segments.narration: Hunter-gatherers built a stone temple before farming existed. Southeastern Turkey, around nine thousand five hundred BC.
The pillars are T-shaped limestone, up to five and a half metres tall, weighing as much as ten tonnes each.
They are covered in carved animals. Foxes, scorpions, vultures, boars. Not hunting scenes. Something closer to a cast list.
There is no pottery here, no writing, no sign of anyone living on site. This was built before all of it.
And then they filled it in. The enclosures were deliberately backfilled with rubble, which is why the carvings survived at all.

verdicts.claim: Göbekli Tepe's monumental enclosures date to roughly the tenth to ninth millennia BCE, before settled agriculture in the region
verdicts.note: 67% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article

verdicts.claim: The site's T-shaped limestone pillars stand up to about 5.5 metres tall and weigh several tonnes
verdicts.note: The largest pillars reach roughly 5.5 m and around 10 tonnes.

verdicts.claim: The pillars carry carved reliefs of animals including foxes, scorpions, vultures and boars
verdicts.note: Relief carvings depict a range of wild animals rather than domesticated species.

verdicts.claim: The site predates pottery and writing and shows limited evidence of permanent domestic occupation
verdicts.note: 74% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article

verdicts.claim: Parts of Göbekli Tepe were deliberately backfilled in antiquity, preserving the carvings
verdicts.note: Intentional burial of enclosures is well attested and explains their preservation.
